definition: Aristocratic means belonging to the privileged, high-born ruling class, a rank inherited by birth rather than gained through wealth or effort.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word aristocratic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know aristocratic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Everything about her manner was aristocratic, from the unhurried way she entered a room to her assumption that doors would simply open for her.
A common family sits at the ordinary center of society with no special rank at all, while an aristocratic one belongs to the hereditary class raised above it.
A genteel household is respectably refined — good manners, a good name — but an aristocratic one adds what gentility alone cannot buy: noble blood and a titled line.

Noble means belonging to a titled ruling class, and it is the plainer, more general word. Aristocratic covers the same inherited rank but leans harder on refinement, pedigree, and a cultivated manner — a family can hold a noble title without seeming especially aristocratic in style.

Patrician emphasizes ancient, established high birth — it originally named Rome's oldest ruling families — so it stresses how long a line has held its standing. Aristocratic is broader, covering the whole privileged class along with its titles and refined bearing, not just the age of the pedigree.

Highborn names the bare fact of birth into the upper class and nothing more. Aristocratic goes beyond the birth itself: it also suggests the rank, privilege, and polished manner that come with belonging to that hereditary class.
Of the common people, outside any noble or ruling class — the direct social opposite of a high-born elite.
Born into a humble, common family — the exact birth-based opposite of aristocratic's inherited high rank.

The riverside club's charter, unchanged since 1721, admitted only families of proven aristocratic descent, turning away the city's wealthiest merchants at the door.
It might be tempting to swap in "elegant" or "wealthy" here, but they miss the point.
A merchant barred from that club could easily be richer and more polished than any member inside.
What kept him out was not a shortage of money or refinement — it was the absence of inherited noble birth.
"aristocratic" specifically means belonging to a hereditary ruling class, a rank you are born into and cannot simply purchase.
"Elegant" describes style and "wealthy" describes money, but only "aristocratic" pins the meaning to lineage — the accident of who your ancestors were.
Formal and literary; common in historical, political, and social writing.
Depending on context it can sound admiring (dignified, refined) or critical (snobbish, elitist), so let the surrounding tone decide which shade you intend.

In 1908 a photographer set up his camera in the lobby of a grand London hotel and began collecting faces.
His subjects were not chosen for beauty.
He wanted the aristocratic guests above all: the families whose names appeared in the peerage registers and whose ease seemed bred rather than learned.
His notebooks show what he was after.
Wealth alone did not interest him; a shipping magnate could buy the same suite and still glance nervously at the staff.
What marked his favorite subjects was inherited certainty -- the unstudied way they wore privilege that had arrived at birth, not through effort.
Modern viewers of the portraits notice it at once.
The difference is not money, the curators like to say.
It is rank absorbed so early that it looks like nature.
